gaps.sentence: Can I ask you ___ questions about your trip?
gaps.hint: polite request with a countable plural
gaps.explanation: 'A few questions' means some questions and is the natural pattern in polite requests.

gaps.sentence: We went to the exhibition, but there was ___ worth seeing.
gaps.explanation: 'But' introduces a contrast, so 'nothing worth seeing' fits the disappointment.

gaps.sentence: ___ of the two proposals has been approved so far.
gaps.explanation: 'Neither of the two' — 'none' is for three or more.

gaps.sentence: ___ of my two brothers work in banking.
gaps.explanation: 'Both of my two brothers work ...' is correct; 'all' and 'none' are not used for two.

gaps.sentence: We had a ___ of fun at the fair.
gaps.explanation: 'A lot of fun' is the fixed phrase; 'fun' is uncountable and the article 'a' forces 'lot'.

gaps.sentence: Hardly ___ came to the afternoon lecture.
gaps.explanation: 'Hardly anyone' is already negative — do not add 'no one'.

gaps.sentence: She made very ___ mistakes in the essay, so she nearly got full marks.
gaps.explanation: 'Very few mistakes' means almost none, which explains the high mark; 'mistakes' is countable.

gaps.sentence: ___ of my friends knew about the concert, so I went on my own.
gaps.explanation: 'None of my friends' means zero friends; 'no' cannot stand before 'of' and 'nothing' is not a quantifier here.
